name: The Five Phases
title: The Five Phases
answer: The Five Phases is a staged method for adopting AI in a school: assess readiness, choose the pilot, set up governance, run and evaluate, and scale what works. Each phase ends with a deliverable a leader can hold, and skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool becomes an expensive disappointment. The higher the stakes of the tool, the slower the phases should go.

sections.body: The Five Phases is a sequence that takes a school from first interest in an AI tool to wider use, with each phase producing a concrete deliverable and a named owner. The problem it solves is adoption that jumps straight to buying or rolling out a tool without checking whether the school is ready, whether the pilot is the right one, or who is accountable. Because every phase ends in something a leader can hold, progress is visible rather than assumed. The text warns that skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool turns into an expensive disappointment. Figure 4.2 in the book lists each phase with its deliverable and owner.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the phases run in order: assess readiness, choose the pilot, set up governance, run and evaluate, then scale what works. The text gives a grade band only in terms of pace rather than year group: a small district can move through the first three phases in a month for a low risk tool such as a lesson planning assistant. A tool that touches student records or decisions about students deserves more time at every step. The rule of thumb is that the higher the stakes, the slower the phases. Each phase still ends with a deliverable and an owner, so leaders can see what has been completed before moving on.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding beyond the reference to Figure 4.2, which lists each phase with its deliverable and owner. It offers the method as practice and a rule of thumb rather than as a research finding. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research as stated in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit the text sets out is that skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool turns into an expensive disappointment, so the sequence should be followed rather than rushed. Pace is the other guardrail: low risk tools can move quickly, while tools that touch student records or decisions about students deserve more time at every step. The higher the stakes, the slower the phases. Decisions about readiness, pilot choice, governance, evaluation and scaling stay with the school's leaders, who own each deliverable. Nothing in the text removes those decisions from people or hands them to the tool.
